title: The Rock on Which the Future Would Be Built
subtitle: The South African diamond fields: Hopetown, Klipdrift, the New Rush and Griqualand West, 1867–1877
intro: In early 1867 a stone picked up by a child on a farm near Hopetown, on the Orange River, travelled by trader's pocket and post envelope to Grahamstown, where a doctor named William Atherstone pronounced it a diamond. Two years later a Griqua shepherd's find, the 83.5-carat Star of South Africa, changed hands for livestock and then for £11,200. By 1870 thousands of diggers were washing gravel on the Vaal at Klipdrift; by July 1871 a cook named Damon had sunk the shaft on a low hill at Vooruitzigt that became the New Rush, then Kimberley, then the deepest hand-dug hole in the world.

The land was claimed by four powers at once. The Griqua under Nicolaas Waterboer held it by treaty and occupation; the Orange Free State had granted the farms on which the dry diggings lay; the South African Republic claimed the north bank of the Vaal; and Tswana chiefs, whose people had lived there longest, were barely heard. Britain resolved the dispute in its own favour: an arbitration award by Robert Keate on 17 October 1871 accepted the Griqua case, and ten days later Sir Henry Barkly proclaimed British sovereignty in Waterboer's name. The Griqua kept almost none of the land.

The diggings became an experiment in controlling labour. White claimholders, organised in diggers' committees and speaking through the camp newspapers, demanded wage cuts, searches, curfews and an end to Black claimholding. In 1872 they burned tents, flogged suspected thieves and won registration rules and a pass law. Meanwhile more than 50,000 African men a year walked to the fields from Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga, Zulu and Tswana country, many to buy guns sold openly in Kimberley. In 1875 the diggers turned on the government itself in the Black Flag rising.

Almost none of this record is diary. It is letters, official papers, an arbitration map, parliamentary answers, newspaper extracts and a few published journals by British visitors. The men who dug the hole left no writing of their own that has been found; their words survive only as complaints and affidavits taken down by officials, and through the reports of Gwayi Tyamzashe, an African minister who came to the fields in 1872. The eyes here are arranged so that the official claim, the diggers' paper and the workers' record can be read against each other on the same days.
calendar_note: All dates are Gregorian, the calendar used by the Cape, the Boer republics and the Griqua government alike. Several key dates (the Atherstone letter, Proclamation 14 of 1872, the 1876 settlement) are known only to the month in the sources used here and are marked approximate.

eyes.name: William Guybon Atherstone
eyes.role: Physician and amateur mineralogist in Grahamstown, aged about 52; the colony's best-known geologist

waypoints.label: Hopetown district: where the stone was picked up

eyes.authenticity: His letter to Lorenzo Boyes at Colesberg is known from its quotation in nineteenth-century accounts and modern histories; the manuscript itself was not consulted. The exact day of the letter is not given in the sources used here.
eyes.bio: A Grahamstown doctor, surgeon and naturalist who had been the first in South Africa to operate under ether. When an envelope arrived from Colesberg holding a pebble that had scratched glass, he tested it and declared it a diamond, overturning a general scepticism. His letter is the first document of the South African diamond age.

sources.title: The shiny stone (account quoting Atherstone's letter)
Eureka Diamond, The Solomon (Kimberley)

eyes.name: James R. Gregory
eyes.role: London mineral and gem dealer sent to investigate the Cape finds
eyes.where: London; visited the Hopetown district in 1868

waypoints.label: London, 20 May 1869: letter to the Geological Magazine

eyes.authenticity: Letters printed in the Geological Magazine (1868–1869). The printed heading gives his initials inconsistently; the substance is not disputed.
eyes.bio: A dealer who toured the Orange River district and reported that the geology made a diamond field impossible, suggesting the stones had been carried in by ostriches or planted. His verdict, repeated after the Star of South Africa had already been found, became a byword for expert error.

sources.title: J. R. Gregory, 'Discovery of diamonds, etc., at the Cape', Geological Magazine, 1869

eyes.name: Richard Southey
eyes.role: Colonial Secretary of the Cape (1864–1872); then Lieutenant-Governor of Griqualand West (January 1873 – August 1875)
eyes.vantage_label: official who claimed the fields, then governed them
eyes.authenticity: Papers and despatches digested in A. Wilmot, The Life and Times of Sir Richard Southey (1904). The famous 'rock' remark is a later tradition: Wilmot records him placing the first diamond on the table of the House of Assembly in 1868, but the exact wording and occasion are not documented in that book.
eyes.bio: The most persistent official advocate of extending British authority over the diamond fields, he drafted the Cape's case against the Free State. As Lieutenant-Governor he tried to balance diggers' demands, the gun trade and African land claims, and was removed after the 1875 rebellion.

sources.title: A. Wilmot, The Life and Times of Sir Richard Southey (1904)

eyes.name: Nicolaas Waterboer
eyes.role: Kaptijn (chief) of the Griqua of Griquatown from 1852
eyes.vantage_label: the chief whose claim the British used
eyes.form: petitions and claims presented through his agent
eyes.language: Dutch / Afrikaans (Cape Dutch); English through his agent
eyes.authenticity: His case survives mostly as presented by his agent David Arnot at the Bloemhof inquiry (the Bloemhof Blue Book, 1871) and as reported in British parliamentary papers. No personal diary is known. No surviving firsthand account in his own hand was found for this chapter.
eyes.bio: Heir to a Griqua polity built on treaties with the Cape, he claimed the land between the Orange and the Vaal. His agent framed the claim so that British rule would follow it; the annexation was made in his name, but most of the land then passed to speculators and the Crown. In 1878 he joined a rising against British rule and was exiled.

sources.title: Nicolaas Waterboer (overview)
Hansard, House of Commons, 19 May 1871
Shillington, The Diamond Fields Dispute

eyes.name: Johannes Henricus Brand
eyes.role: State President of the Orange Free State (1864–1888)
eyes.vantage_label: president of the state that lost the dry diggings
eyes.authenticity: His despatches to the Cape governor are summarised in British parliamentary answers; Free State Volksraad protests survive in printed copies. The 1876 settlement terms are well documented in secondary histories.
eyes.bio: A Cape-trained lawyer who led the Free State for 24 years. Dutoitspan, Bultfontein and the farm Vooruitzigt lay on land the Free State had granted and policed, and he refused to submit his title to arbitration. He chose protest and negotiation over war, and in 1876 accepted £90,000 in compensation.

sources.title: Hansard, House of Commons, 19 May 1871 (summary of Brand's despatch of 28 March 1871)

eyes.name: Robert William Keate
eyes.role: Lieutenant-Governor of Natal; arbitrator in the Vaal River dispute
eyes.authenticity: The Award and its accompanying map (dated 17 October 1871) were printed with the Bloemhof evidence and survive in the Cape Surveyor-General's maps.
eyes.bio: A colonial governor appointed to settle the dispute if the two Bloemhof commissioners disagreed. He never visited the fields; he read the evidence and drew a line that favoured the Griqua and Tswana claimants against the South African Republic, a line that made annexation possible.

sources.title: Sketch of the Territories on the Vaal River to accompany the Award of R. W. Keate, 17 October 1871

eyes.name: Sir Henry Barkly
eyes.role: Governor of the Cape Colony and High Commissioner (1870–1877)
eyes.where: Cape Town; visited the fields 1871 and 1872
eyes.authenticity: Letters to Southey quoted in Wilmot (1904); his speech to the Cape Parliament of 18 April 1872 is known here through a later translated compilation, so its wording is not quoted.
eyes.bio: A former sugar planter and experienced governor who arrived in January 1871 and set up the Bloemhof inquiry. He proclaimed British sovereignty over the fields in October 1871 and spent the next year insisting the diggers consented, while their newspapers said otherwise.

sources.title: Wilmot, Life and Times of Sir Richard Southey
Reitz, A Century of Wrong, Appendix B (translated extracts)

eyes.name: The diggings press: Diamond News, Diamond Field and Diggers' Gazette
eyes.role: Newspapers printed on the fields for the white digging public
eyes.side: White diggers (British, colonial, Free State and foreign)
eyes.where: Klipdrift and Pniel, then Dutoitspan and New Rush
eyes.authenticity: A collective editorial voice, not one diarist. Dated extracts are known here through Reitz's compilation (in retranslation, so not quoted) and through citations in Sieborger (1975) and Meredith (2007). Original files survive in South African libraries.
eyes.bio: The camp papers spoke for claimholders: against Cape taxation and the annexation, for harsher control of African labour, and loudest about theft. Read against the grain, they record wage cuts, mob justice and the arrival and departure of thousands of workers.

sources.title: Reitz, A Century of Wrong, Appendix B
Sieborger, The Recruitment and Organisation of African Labour for the Kimberley Diamond Mines 1871–1888 (MA, Rhodes, 1975)

eyes.name: Cecil John Rhodes
eyes.role: English vicar's son, aged 17–18; cotton farmer in Natal, then digger at Colesberg Kopje
eyes.where: Natal, then Dutoitspan and New Rush
eyes.authenticity: Letters to his mother, printed in early biographies (Michell 1910; Williams 1921) and held among the Rhodes papers at the Bodleian Library. Quoted here through Meredith (2007).
eyes.bio: Sent to Natal for his health, he reached the diamond fields in November 1871 with his brother Herbert's claims to work. His early letters are a young man's mix of measurement, money and wonder; within twenty years the same hole was the base of his monopoly.

sources.title: South African History Online: Cecil John Rhodes

eyes.name: Frederick Boyle
eyes.role: English journalist and travel writer, aged 30, who bought into a claim
eyes.authenticity: Published as To the Cape for Diamonds (London: Chapman and Hall, 1873), largely in diary form. Specific dates here follow Meredith's citations; the volume itself was not consulted.
eyes.bio: A professional traveller who came to write and stayed to dig. He paid £365 for a quarter-claim in December 1871 and recorded the price collapse of January 1872 as it hit the camp.

sources.title: To the Cape for Diamonds (1873), catalogue record

eyes.name: Gwayi Tyamzashe
eyes.role: Xhosa minister trained at Lovedale, aged 28 on arrival; pastor to African workers at the fields
eyes.vantage_label: an African pastor among the workers
eyes.authenticity: Letter to Dr James Stewart of Lovedale (30 November 1872) in the Stewart papers; article 'Life at the Diamond Fields', Kaffir Express, 1874, reprinted in F. Wilson and D. Perrot, Outlook on a Century (1973). Content summarised here from secondary citations; the original text was not consulted.
eyes.bio: One of the first ordained African ministers, he arrived in October 1872 and stayed more than a decade. He is the closest the record comes to an African eyewitness who wrote about the fields as they were forming, and he wrote as a Christian critic of drink and disorder as well as an observer of the many peoples gathered there.

sources.title: Kimberley City Info: Gway Tyamzashe
Sieborger thesis (1975)

eyes.name: Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga and other African migrant workers
eyes.role: Men who walked hundreds of miles to dig for wages, usually for three to six months
eyes.side: Pedi, Sotho, Tsonga ('Shangaan'), Zulu, Tswana and others
eyes.where: The diggings and the roads to them
eyes.vantage_label: the labour that dug the hole
eyes.form: official records (affidavits, complaints, registrations) and press reports about them
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. Their words survive only as complaints and affidavits taken down by Griqualand West officials and as reports in the white press, cited in Sieborger (1975).
eyes.bio: By the early 1870s more than 50,000 Africans a year came to the fields. Many were sent or allowed by their chiefs to earn guns, which could be bought openly at Kimberley. They faced wage cuts, searches, passes, floggings and attacks on the road home.

sources.title: Sieborger thesis (1975)
Potenza, 'All that glitters'

eyes.name: Damon (probably Esau Demoense)
eyes.role: Coloured cook in Fleetwood Rawstorne's 'Colesberg party'
eyes.where: Colesberg Kopje on the farm Vooruitzigt
eyes.vantage_label: the man who dug the first stones of the New Rush
eyes.authenticity: No surviving firsthand account found. Henry Giddy and Fleetwood Rawstorne named him as the finder; his identification with Esau Demoense rests on a 1974 family interview and is an inference.
eyes.bio: Sent by Rawstorne to sink a shaft on the low hill, he brought up the stones that started the richest rush of all. The claims were registered in his employer's party's names.

sources.title: Today in Kimberley's History, 16 July

eyes.name: Anthony Trollope
eyes.role: English novelist, aged 62, on a tour of South Africa
eyes.authenticity: South Africa (2 vols, London 1878), written during and just after his tour of 1877; public domain on Project Gutenberg.
eyes.bio: Trollope reached Kimberley in the latter part of 1877, when the open pit was already the wonder of the colony. He admired the engineering, doubted the British title to the land and wrote about African workers with the prejudices of his class.

sources.title: Trollope, South Africa, vol. II (Project Gutenberg)
Excerpt, Internet Modern History Sourcebook

entries.date_display: March 1867 (exact day of letter not established)
entries.headline: A pebble from the Orange River proves to be a diamond
entries.digest: An envelope came from Lorenzo Boyes, acting Civil Commissioner at Colesberg, holding a stone a farm child near Hopetown had picked up as a plaything. The trader John O'Reilly had carried it to Colesberg, where it scratched glass. Atherstone tested its hardness and specific gravity and wrote back that it was a true diamond of more than 21 carats, worth about £500, and asked whether he should send it on to the Colonial Secretary.
entries.quote: It is a veritable diamond, weighs twenty-one and a quarter carats
entries.source_note: Letter to Boyes as quoted in 'The shiny stone' and in The Solomon's Eureka page; month from the brief and from the Cape Argus report of 18 April 1867.

entries.headline: The government holds a Hopetown stone and plans to test it in London
entries.digest: The Cape government, through the Colonial Office that Southey ran, now had the stone. A Cape Town diamond cutter and polisher agreed with Atherstone; the Cape Argus reported the find with a value of £500 rough and £800 cut, and said it would go to London for a final test. Governor Wodehouse later bought it at Atherstone's valuation, and it was shown at the Paris Exhibition that year.
entries.source_note: Cape Argus, 18 April 1867, reprinted in the Southland Times, 2 August 1867 (Papers Past).

entries.headline: A London dealer finds no diamond country
entries.digest: Gregory travelled up from the coast to inspect the district where the stones were said to come from. He saw nothing in the rocks that resembled known diamond ground and concluded that the reports were exaggerated or that the stones had been brought in from elsewhere. His report was printed in London and cooled interest in the trade.
entries.source_note: Geological Magazine vol. V (1868), referred to in his letter of 20 May 1869.

entries.headline: Southey lays a diamond on the table of the House
entries.digest: Wilmot's life of Southey records that he placed the first diamond found on the table of the House of Assembly in 1868. Later tradition attaches to this scene, or to the Star of South Africa in 1869, the words that the stone was the rock on which South Africa's future would be built. The wording and occasion are not documented in the sources consulted.
entries.quote: rock on which the future success of South Africa will be built
entries.source_note: Wilmot (1904), account of the 1868 session; the phrase is a later popular attribution (title of Potenza, SAHO) and is not documented in Wilmot.

entries.headline: Two months after the Star, Gregory still says impossible
entries.digest: Writing to the Geological Magazine, Gregory restated that the geology of the Orange River country ruled out a diamond field and called the Cape newspaper reports grossly exaggerated. By then the 83.5-carat stone later called the Star of South Africa had been bought at Hopetown for £11,200. His letter became the classic example of expert certainty overtaken by events.
entries.quote: impossible that any diamonds could really have been found there
entries.source_note: J. R. Gregory, letter dated 20 May 1869, Geological Magazine (Cambridge Core PDF).

entries.headline: A seventeen-year-old sees Rolleston's diamonds
entries.digest: Newly landed in Natal to join his brother's cotton farm, Rhodes met Captain Loftus Rolleston, whose party had struck diamond gravel on the Vaal in January. He wrote to his mother that the sight of the stones made his mouth water, and listed three big ones valued at £8,000 to £10,000. The fields were still a rumour four hundred miles away.
entries.source_note: Letter to his mother, September 1870, as quoted in Meredith, Diamonds, Gold and War (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: The Griqua chief asks for British protection
entries.digest: With diggers pouring onto the Vaal and the Free State and the South African Republic both claiming the land, Waterboer's agent Arnot pressed his title to the country between the Orange and the Vaal and asked that it be placed under the Queen. Arnot also issued land titles himself and hoped to sell farms to British settlers. In London the government told Parliament that Waterboer strongly wished his country to come under British rule.
entries.source_note: Shillington, The Diamond Fields Dispute; Hansard, House of Commons, 19 May 1871.

entries.headline: Southey argues the case against the Free State
entries.digest: As Barkly arrived to deal with the dispute, Southey produced a memorandum answering the Orange Free State's claim to the fields. It rested the British case on Griqua title and earlier boundary rulings. Cape opinion was divided; the Assembly later backed annexation only by a majority of two.
entries.source_note: Memorandum of 20 January 1871 and 1871 session, in Wilmot (1904).

entries.headline: Brand defends Free State burghers on the disputed ground
entries.digest: Brand refused to submit the Free State's title to the Bloemhof arbitration and Free State forces had moved into part of the disputed territory. Replying to Barkly's protest, he wrote that they had entered only to protect the rights of Free State subjects, and that he would lay the matter before the Volksraad on 3 April.
entries.quote: to protect the rights of Free State subjects
entries.source_note: Brand's despatch of 28 March 1871 as summarised in the House of Commons, 19 May 1871 (Hansard).

entries.headline: London cites Waterboer's wish to accept British rule
entries.digest: Answering a question in the Commons, the colonial under-secretary said the many British subjects on the fields made settled government an absolute necessity, and that the Griqua chief had offered his territory. The Queen had been advised to accept the offer pending arbitration. Waterboer's own words do not appear in the record; his claim reached London as Arnot and the Cape framed it.
entries.quote: absolute necessity for the establishment of some settled government
entries.source_note: Hansard, HC Deb 19 May 1871, vol. 206, cc1037–9.

entries.date_display: Sunday 16 July 1871 (15 and 17 July also given)
entries.headline: The cook's shaft on the low hill yields diamonds
entries.digest: Fleetwood Rawstorne, of a party from Colesberg, sent his cook Damon to dig on a low ironstone hill on the De Beers' farm, where an earlier shaft had produced nothing. Damon came back with diamonds. The party pegged the first claims; two days later the hill was rushed by thousands. It became the New Rush, then the Kimberley Mine, then the Big Hole.
entries.source_note: Today in Kimberley's History, 16 July (dates from Beet, Giddy and Kisch); Damon named by Giddy and Rawstorne.

entries.headline: The arbitrator draws the line for the Griqua
entries.digest: Keate delivered his Award on the boundary north of the Vaal between the South African Republic and the Griqua, Barolong, Bangwaketse and Batlhaping. On the evidence Arnot had marshalled at Bloemhof, he found for the African claimants. The map that went with it shows the Griqua boundary that annexation would adopt.
entries.source_note: Award map dated 17 October 1871, Cape Surveyor-General's Office (Africa Commons).

entries.headline: Britain proclaims the diamond fields its own
entries.digest: Ten days after the Award, Barkly proclaimed British sovereignty over Griqualand West, including the dry diggings that the Free State had held. Officials hoisted the flag on the fields; the Free State police withdrew. Barkly told the Cape Parliament the diggers had consented, which their papers disputed.
entries.source_note: SAHO dated event (27 October 1871); Wilmot (1904) on Campbell's report of 20 November 1871.

entries.headline: His land annexed in his name
entries.digest: The proclamation made Waterboer's territory British. In practice it ended Griqua control: land titles that Arnot and others had issued passed to speculators, and the diamond farms stayed with their white owners. No statement by Waterboer from that day survives in the sources consulted.
entries.source_note: Shillington; Nicolaas Waterboer overview; Diamond News, 8 October 1872, on land claims held by Arnot and Orpen.

entries.headline: The Free State protests the seizure
entries.digest: The Free State Volksraad and Brand protested the annexation as a breach of the Free State's title, since farms such as Dutoitspan, Bultfontein and Vooruitzigt had been granted under Free State law. Brand chose protest over war and asked for the dispute to go to foreign arbitration, which Britain refused.
entries.source_note: Printed copies of the Volksraad protest exist (auction record); Hansard 1871 for his earlier position; month approximate.

entries.headline: Rhodes reaches the dry diggings
entries.digest: After more than a month by horse and ox-cart from Natal, Rhodes arrived at Dutoitspan and moved to his brother's claims on Colesberg Kopje. Herbert left for England a couple of weeks later, leaving Cecil, at eighteen, to work them with hired African labour.
entries.source_note: Meredith (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: The Diamond News chokes on the dust
entries.digest: A correspondent of the Diamond News complained of the dust of the dry diggings, which coated tents, food and lungs. The New Rush had already produced some £50,000 of diamonds a week in August, and the yellow ground was nearly worked out.
entries.source_note: Diamond News, November 1871, cited in Meredith (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: Camps left to defend themselves
entries.digest: The Diamond News complained that when the Free State police withdrew, the camps had to look after themselves again, and that the new Cape administration was no improvement. The paper spoke for diggers who resented both Boer and British authority.
entries.source_note: Diamond News, 16 December 1871, translated extract in Reitz, A Century of Wrong, Appendix B.

entries.headline: A journalist buys a quarter-claim
entries.digest: Boyle paid £365 for a quarter of a claim, some fifteen feet square of ground on the kopje. Prices were at their height and the hill was a honeycomb of square pits with narrow roadways between them.
entries.source_note: To the Cape for Diamonds (1873), cited in Meredith (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: Ant-heaps, and thirty carats a week
entries.digest: Rhodes described the kopje to his mother as a crowd of ant-heaps, black with men, and gave figures: about 30 carats a week, worth roughly £100. The letter is all practical detail of claims, sieves and prices, from a boy who had become a small employer.
entries.source_note: Letter to his mother, 4 January 1872, quoted in Meredith (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: News of a price crash reaches the camp
entries.digest: Boyle's diary recorded the panic when word came that diamond prices had collapsed in London under the weight of Cape stones. Buyers held off, claimholders who had paid high prices faced ruin, and the mood of the camp changed overnight.
entries.source_note: Boyle's diary entry for 13 January 1872, cited in Meredith (2007), ch. 2.

entries.headline: Diggers demand laws to control African labour
entries.digest: White residents of the fields called for written contracts for servants, the right to search them at any time, a night curfew and an end to digging licences for Black and Coloured men unless fifty white claimholders vouched for them. The papers presented theft as the cause; Black claimholders were the target.
entries.source_note: Meredith (2007), ch. 5.

entries.headline: The governor tells Parliament the diggers consent
entries.digest: Opening the Cape Parliament, Barkly said British sovereignty had been proclaimed with the full agreement of the diggers and that the new administration worked well. Within two weeks the Diamond News called this blind to rising discontent, and the Diamond Field reckoned the fields nine to one against being joined to the Cape.
entries.source_note: Speech of 18 April 1872; Diamond News 1 May 1872; Diamond Field 30 May 1872 (translated extracts in Reitz, Appendix B).

entries.headline: Nine hundred workers walk away from a wage cut
entries.digest: After a letter in the Diamond News urged a cut of a quarter or more, diggers' meetings resolved to reduce African wages to five or six shillings a week, paid monthly. Reports said about 900 Africans left the fields in two days. Leaving was the one sanction workers held; none of their own words about it are recorded.
entries.source_note: Diamond News 15 May 1872; meetings including De Beers, 8 June 1872, chaired by Alfred Aylward; departures 6 June 1872 (Sieborger 1975).

entries.headline: A worker dies after a flogging in the cold
entries.digest: A white digger flogged two Black workers he suspected of theft and left them tied outside on a winter night; one died. The court convicted him only of common assault and gave six months' hard labour. That month mobs burned tents of Black claimholders and of men accused of buying stolen diamonds.
entries.source_note: Meredith (2007), ch. 5.

entries.headline: Mass meetings, and a hope the fire will die down
entries.digest: The day after a Market Square meeting demanded changes in the law against theft by labourers and illicit buying, the Diamond News described tense mass meetings and hoped the unrest would soon be brought under control. The Diggers' Gazette warned that lynch law had taken over at New Rush. On 22 July another meeting defended the sale of rifles to Africans, which kept labour coming.
entries.source_note: Diamond News 20 July 1872; Diggers' Gazette 26 July 1872 (Reitz, Appendix B); meeting of 22 July 1872 (Sieborger).

entries.headline: Registration of servants begins
entries.digest: Government Notice No. 68 set up a system of registering African servants, with a fee of one shilling. It was the first step toward the pass regime that followed within weeks.
entries.source_note: Government Notice No. 68 of 23 July 1872 (Sieborger 1975).

entries.headline: Passes, warrantless search and the lash
entries.digest: Proclamation 14 of 1872 created a master-and-servant code for the fields. An African found without a pass could be fined £5, jailed for up to three months or flogged, and employers could search servants without a warrant. The rules applied by race, not by whether a man was a servant or a claimholder.
entries.source_note: Proclamation 14 of 1872 as described in Meredith (2007), ch. 5; month as given there.

entries.headline: Barkly at New Rush asks Southey to take over
entries.digest: Visiting the fields, Barkly wrote to Southey offering him charge of Griqualand West's government. On 17 October he renewed the offer as Administrator, as an alternative to a post in the new Cape ministry. Southey, who had retired as Colonial Secretary that year, took the fields.
entries.source_note: Barkly to Southey, New Rush, 14 September 1872, and note of 17 October 1872, in Wilmot (1904).

entries.headline: Who owns the kopjes? Arnot and Orpen
entries.digest: The Diamond News charged that the claims and the kopjes had all been provided for, with land titles concentrated in the hands of Waterboer's agent David Arnot and the surveyor Francis Orpen. Earlier it had joked that the real head chief of Griqualand West was Arnot, not Waterboer.
entries.source_note: Diamond News, 8 October 1872 (translated extract in Reitz, Appendix B).

entries.headline: A Lovedale minister arrives at the diggings
entries.digest: Sent by the Lovedale mission, Tyamzashe reached the fields to minister to African Christians among the workers. He found men from almost every people of southern Africa crowded into the camps.
entries.source_note: Arrival date 19.10.1872 in Sieborger (1975).

entries.headline: First report home to Lovedale
entries.digest: Six weeks after arriving, Tyamzashe wrote to Dr James Stewart at Lovedale about his work at the fields. The letter is cited by historians of labour on the fields; its text was not available for this chapter.
entries.source_note: Letter to Stewart, 30 November 1872, cited in Sieborger (1975); content not consulted.

entries.headline: Sotho workers fired on going home
entries.digest: A Free State burgher commando fired on about 80 Sotho men returning from the fields with their earnings, killing two. The Sotho fired back and retreated to Kimberley. Workers who walked home with guns crossed hostile ground.
entries.source_note: Diamond News, 4 February 1873, cited in Sieborger (1975).

entries.headline: Southey takes up the government of the fields
entries.digest: Southey arrived to govern Griqualand West, which that year received a constitution with a Legislative Council of eight, four elected. He inherited the labour laws of 1872 and an open gun trade on which the supply of workers depended.
entries.source_note: Term January 1873 to August 1875 (Sieborger 1975); constitution (Meredith 2007, ch. 5).

entries.headline: A tax on guns, not a ban
entries.digest: Southey's administration issued Proclamation No. 12 of 1873, taxing guns and gun barrels sold on the fields. The trade continued: tens of thousands of guns went home with workers in the following year.
entries.source_note: Proclamation No. 12 of 1873, 19 March 1873 (Sieborger 1975).

entries.headline: Ordained at New Rush, days before it becomes Kimberley
entries.digest: Tyamzashe was ordained at the Mutual Hall, New Rush. Two days later the camp took the name Kimberley, after the Colonial Secretary in London, Lord Kimberley, who had disliked the old names.
entries.source_note: Kimberley City Info, Tyamzashe profile; renaming 5 July 1873 (The Solomon).

entries.headline: Three Sotho men complain to the Lieutenant-Governor
entries.digest: Three Sotho workers told Southey that eight armed Boers had stopped them on the road and taken their guns and property. The complaint was written down by officials; it is one of the few places where workers' own account of the journey home survives. In the same season Zulu workers recruited for the fields swore affidavits that they had been arrested and robbed in the Free State.
entries.source_note: Complaint of September 1873 and affidavits of 30 August and 2 September 1873 (Sieborger 1975).

entries.headline: 'Life at the Diamond Fields' in the Kaffir Express
entries.digest: Tyamzashe published an account of the fields in the Lovedale paper. He wrote of the mixture of peoples there, noting that within a year of the mines opening almost every society of the subcontinent except the Zulu and Venda was represented, and of the drinking, gambling and Sunday labour that troubled him as a minister.
entries.source_note: Article as reprinted in Outlook on a Century (1973); content via Potenza (SAHO) and Kimberley City Info; details of the text not checked against the original.

entries.headline: The black flag over Kimberley
entries.digest: When William Cowie was convicted of selling guns to the diggers' leader Alfred Aylward without a permit, a black flag was raised on the debris heap called Mount Ararat. Armed diggers' companies held the streets for weeks. Southey, with no troops of his own, asked for British soldiers.
entries.source_note: Black Flag Revolt (overview); Meredith (2007), ch. 5.

entries.headline: Troops arrive; Southey is let go
entries.digest: British troops marched in after a journey of some 700 miles and met no resistance. A local jury acquitted the rebel leaders in twenty-three minutes. The Colonial Office blamed Southey for the cost and relieved him in August 1875.
entries.source_note: Black Flag Revolt (overview); Meredith (2007), ch. 5.

entries.headline: Brand takes £90,000 for the dry diggings
entries.digest: Brand travelled to London and settled the Free State's claim to the diamond fields for £90,000 in compensation. The Free State gave up its title to Kimberley and the dry diggings without a war.
entries.source_note: Standard secondary accounts of the 1876 settlement; month approximate.

entries.headline: The largest hole ever made by man
entries.digest: Trollope stood at the rim of the Kimberley mine, now some 230 feet deep and 300 yards across, with buckets running on wires to the bottom. He counted between 3,500 and 4,000 African workers paid about ten shillings a week and food, and repeated the employers' view that they stole for their chiefs. In the same book he wrote that he was not at ease with the title by which Britain had taken the land.
entries.quote: the largest and most complete hole ever made by human agency
entries.source_note: Trollope, South Africa (1878), vol. II, chs. VII–VIII (Project Gutenberg; Fordham excerpt).

entries.headline: Waterboer joins a rising and is exiled
entries.digest: Seven years after the annexation made in his name, Waterboer took part in the Griqua and Tlhaping rising against British rule in Griqualand West. He was arrested and sent into exile at Hopetown, near the farm where the first diamond had been found, and was allowed back in 1880.
entries.source_note: Nicolaas Waterboer overview.

convergences.label: The first diamond is named and handed to the state
convergences.note: Atherstone's test turned a child's plaything into colonial property within weeks; the government's first instinct was to send it to London for a verdict.

convergences.label: The Star of South Africa versus the London expert
convergences.note: While Southey's colony was showing off Cape diamonds, Gregory was still writing that a diamond field there was impossible.

convergences.label: The Award and the annexation
convergences.note: Keate drew the line on paper, Barkly proclaimed it, Waterboer's name justified it, and Brand lost the dry diggings his state had granted and policed.

convergences.label: Newcomers at the kopje
convergences.note: An eighteen-year-old, a London journalist and the camp paper describe the same dusty honeycomb in the months after the New Rush.

convergences.label: The January price collapse
convergences.note: Rhodes, writing on 4 January, still counts carats and pounds; nine days later Boyle records the panic as London prices fall.

convergences.label: The July crisis: mobs, wage cuts and registration
convergences.note: The papers wrote of theft and lynch law; the official record shows a flogging death, burned tents and the first registration rules. The workers' answer was to leave.

convergences.label: A new government and a new pastor
convergences.note: While Barkly recruited Southey and the Diamond News attacked Arnot's land claims, Tyamzashe arrived to minister to the men the new laws were written for.

convergences.label: Southey's first year
convergences.note: The Lieutenant-Governor taxed guns and heard the complaints of Sotho men robbed on the road; at New Rush, renamed Kimberley, Tyamzashe was ordained.

convergences.label: Coda: rebellion, compensation, reflection (1875–1877)
convergences.note: The diggers' rising cost Southey his post, Brand took £90,000, and Trollope wondered aloud whether the title had ever been good.

ties.note: Atherstone's letter asked whether the stone should go to Southey as Colonial Secretary; the Colonial Office then handled it.
The London dealer's verdict that the district could hold no diamonds directly contradicted Atherstone's identification and the colony's hopes.
Barkly relied on Southey's case against the Free State and in 1872 wrote from New Rush asking him to govern the fields.
Keate's Award accepted the Griqua and Tswana evidence that Waterboer's agent assembled at Bloemhof.
Both claimed the land between the Orange and Vaal; the British used Waterboer's title to override the Free State's grants.
Barkly protested Free State occupation of the disputed ground in 1871; Brand refused his arbitration and protested the annexation.
Barkly claimed the diggers' consent to annexation; the Diamond News and Diamond Field said the fields were overwhelmingly against Cape rule.
The camp papers campaigned for wage cuts, searches and passes; the workers' recorded response was mass departure.
Sotho workers brought their complaints of robbery on the road to Southey in 1873; his administration also taxed the guns they bought.
Tyamzashe lived and preached among the African workers of New Rush and wrote about the many peoples gathered there.
Rhodes's claims were on the kopje where Damon's shaft had found the first stones four months earlier.
The Diamond News mocked the idea that Waterboer ruled anything and accused his agent Arnot of holding the land claims.
Trollope's chapter on why Britain took Griqualand West questioned the purchase-based title derived from the Griqua chief.

claims.claim: Hopetown stone (later the Eureka) identified as a diamond of 21.25 carats, valued at £500.
claims.evidence: Atherstone's letter to Boyes, as quoted in later accounts

claims.claim: Government holds the stone; valued at £500 rough, £800 cut; to be sent to London for final test.
claims.evidence: Cape Argus, 18 April 1867, reprinted Southland Times 2 Aug 1867

claims.claim: Star of South Africa: 83.5 carats rough, obtained from a Griqua shepherd (named in some accounts as Swartbooi) by Schalk van Niekerk for 500 sheep, 10 oxen and a horse; sold at Hopetown for £11,200. Who owned the stone and the ground it came from was not recorded as a question.
claims.evidence: Meredith (2007); The Solomon, Star of South Africa

claims.claim: Expert denial: geology makes a Cape diamond field impossible; press reports grossly exaggerated.
Griqua claim to the land between the Orange and Vaal, with a request for British protection, presented by agent David Arnot.
Free State position: its burghers entered the disputed territory to protect the rights of Free State subjects; Free State refuses arbitration.
claims.evidence: Brand's despatch as reported in Hansard, 19 May 1871

claims.claim: First diamonds on Colesberg Kopje, found by the cook Damon; claims registered by Rawstorne's Colesberg party. Priority dated variously by Giddy (15th), Beet (16th) and Kisch (17th).
Colesberg Kopje yielding about £50,000 of diamonds a week; some 10,000 men at work at Vooruitzigt within two months of May.
Keate Award: boundary north of the Vaal fixed in favour of Griqua, Barolong, Bangwaketse and Batlhaping against the South African Republic.
British sovereignty proclaimed over Griqualand West, river and dry diggings included.
A quarter-claim on Colesberg Kopje bought for £365.
claims.evidence: Boyle, To the Cape for Diamonds (1873), via Meredith

claims.claim: About 30 carats a week from the Rhodes claims, worth roughly £100.
claims.evidence: Letter to his mother, via Meredith (2007)

claims.claim: Diggers' meetings set African wages at 5s.–6s. a week; about 900 Africans reported leaving in two days.
claims.evidence: Diamond News and meeting reports, cited in Sieborger (1975)

claims.claim: Proclamation 14: pass required; penalty £5, up to three months' prison, or flogging; search without warrant.
About 75,000 guns sold at Kimberley, mostly to African workers; old Enfields about £3, Sniders about £12.
Free State claim to the diamond fields settled for £90,000 compensation.

threads_out.note: Capital, men and methods moved from Kimberley to the Rand: Rhodes, J. B. Robinson, Wernher and Beit took diamond fortunes to the gold reef, and the pass and compound systems first tried at Kimberley shaped labour there.
The Cullinan was found in a kimberlite pipe, the rock type named after Kimberley's mine, and entered a world diamond market that De Beers, built on the Kimberley claims, had organised.
Both chapters turn on who owned a stone and the land it came from: a Punjab treaty surrendered the Koh-i-Noor to the Crown, and a Griqua title let the Crown take the diamond fields.
Diggers from California and Australia brought claim sizes, diggers' committees and the habit of self-made law to the Vaal; the Kimberley diggers' committees echoed the mining camps of 1849.
The Griqua and Tswana country annexed in 1871 lay on the missionary road north through Kuruman that Livingstone had taken; the same year, Stanley found him at Ujiji.
